title: Game 7: Magnus vs Hans
notes: Game 7 of 12 in the experiment, from the French Defence. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

This is the French Classical; 4.e5 gains space and kicks the knight to d7 with tempo, and I checked that e5 is defended by the d4 pawn so nothing captures it profitably. No Black check or capture is available after it, so my king's safety and material are intact.

This is the Steinitz Variation of the French Defence, where the knight must retreat since it's attacked by the e5 pawn; Nfd7 is the main line, keeping the knight active and preparing to hit e5 with c5 and Nc6. Ne4 loses a piece to Nxe4, and Ng4 leaves the knight loose after h3.

This is the French Steinitz, where 5.f4 is the main line, reinforcing the e5 wedge and gaining space before Black can hit it with ...c5 or ...f6. I checked Rule 1: f4 does open e1-h4, but 5...Qh4+ 6.g3 simply chases the queen with a free tempo, so there is no danger.

This is the Steinitz French, and the main line is to strike at the overextended center immediately with c5, hitting d4 before White consolidates with Nf3 and Be3. Alternatives like c6 or f6 are too passive or premature; after c5 6.Nf3 Nc6 I get good pressure, and 6.dxc5 Nc6 lets me regain the pawn with a fine game.

This is the main-line French Steinitz; 6.Nf3 develops, guards d4 and prepares Be3/Be2 with castling, and I checked that Nxd5 simply loses a piece to exd5. Black's best replies (...Nc6 or ...cxd4 7.Nxd4) give me nothing to fear — no checks on e1-h4 since d4/f4 are covered and ...Qb6 is met by Na4 or Be3.

This is the French Steinitz with 5.f4; the main line is to pile pressure on d4 immediately, and 6...Nc6 develops while hitting the center (after 7.Be3 cxd4 8.Nxd4 Bc5 I get good play). I avoided 6...Nxe5 7.fxe5 which just drops a piece, and 6...Qh4+ 7.g3 only loses time.

Nxd5 is a trap since exd5 just wins the knight, so I checked the capture first and rejected it. Instead 7.Be3 is the main-line move: it develops, adds a third defender to the d4 pawn so ...cxd4 or ...Qb6 gains nothing, and keeps my e5 wedge supported by f4 while Black has no checks available.

This is the French Steinitz with 5.f4; the thematic move is to pile pressure on the d4 pawn before White consolidates. 7...Qb6 hits d4 and b2 simultaneously, and after 8.Na4 Qa5+ 9.c3 c4 or 8.Qd2 cxd4 9.Nxd4 Nxd4 I get comfortable play, whereas 7...cxd4 8.Nxd4 just releases the tension and hands White a strong centre.

This is the main line of the Steinitz French, where 8.Na4 hits the loose queen and the c5 pawn; crucially it also removes the Qb6-b2 threat because 8...cxd4 now runs into 9.Nxb6 winning the queen, so Black must spend time with 8...Qa5+ (which I block with 9.c3) or retreat. I checked that Na4 is attacked by nothing and that d4 remains defended three times (Be3, Nf3, Qd1) against its three attackers, so no recapture sequence loses material.

White's knight on a4 is completely undefended (the queen's d1–a4 diagonal is blocked by the c2 pawn), so I check on a5 where my queen also eyes the knight down the a-file. Only 9.Nc3 saves the piece — 9.c3, 9.Bd2, 9.Nd2, 9.Qd2 or 9.b4 all allow 9...Qxa4, and after 10.b3 my queen escapes via a6/b5 a whole piece up; a5 is also safer than b4, where a3 would immediately kick me.

Black's Qa5+ both checks along the a5-e1 diagonal and attacks my undefended knight on a4, so any blocking move (c3, b4, Bd2, Qd2) or king step loses the knight to Qxa4 (b4 even drops a pawn with check). Only the knight itself can block and save itself: Nc3 lands on a square guarded by both b2 and Qd1, so Qxc3 or Bb4 pressure costs Black nothing but gains nothing.

White's Na4-c3 shuffle lost two tempi, so I should strike at the centre immediately while his king is still uncastled. 9...cxd4 10.Nxd4 Bb4 pins the knight with my queen already on a5, and after 10...Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bb4 I get fast development with pressure on c3. The e5-sacrifices (Ndxe5) just lose material after fxe5.

Black's cxd4 hits my Be3, so I must resolve the d4 pawn; 10.Nxd4 is the cleanest since 10...Nxd4 11.Bxd4 keeps everything defended (Bd4 guards e5 and Qd1 guards d4), and the tactical try 10...Ncxe5 11.fxe5 Qxe5 is met by 12.Qd2, defending both e3 and d4 while I stay a piece up. Crucially, keeping the knight on c3 blocks the a5-e1 diagonal so ...Bb4 is never a check.

Qxc3+ just loses the queen to bxc3, and the e5 pawn is well defended by f4, so I'll relieve the central tension by trading off White's strong d4 knight. After Nxd4 Bxd4 I can follow up with Bb4 or Nb6, piling on the c3 knight and White's centre.

I'm temporarily a knight down after ...Nxd4, so I must recapture, and rule 7 says prefer the minor piece: Bxd4 restores material while keeping my queen home and covering the dark squares. I checked Black's replies: ...Qxc3+ fails to bxc3, ...Qxa2 is met by Rxa2, and ...Nxe5 just drops a piece to fxe5; my king on e1 stays safe since Nc3 blocks the a5-e1 diagonal.

Taking the a2 pawn looks greedy — after 12.Ra1 or 12.Nb5 my queen gets harassed while White develops with threats, and 11...Nxe5 just drops a piece to fxe5. Instead Bb4 develops with tempo, pins the c3 knight against the king on the b4–e1 diagonal, and prepares castling; if 12.a3 I can take on c3 and win the pawn back with Qxc3+.

Black's Bb4 and Qa5 aim at my pinned Nc3, and the threat is Bxc3+ bxc3 Qxc3+ followed by Qxa1 since my rook is loose — so a3, Rb1 or Rc1 (c2 blocks the file) all fail to truly cover c3. Qd2 defends the knight, shields the e1–b4 diagonal, and offers a queen trade: Qxd2+ Kxd2 Bxc3+ bxc3 leaves me with the bishop pair and central space, while any other black try keeps my material intact.

White's 12.Qd2 left the a2 pawn undefended, and after Qxa2 the rook on a1 is also attacked and undefended, so White must spend a tempo on it — and tries like 13.Nb5 or 13.Nxd5 run into 13...Qxa1+ winning the rook, since b1-c1-d1 are all empty. I checked Nxe5 instead, but after fxe5 Bxc3 bxc3 Qxe5+ I end up giving two pieces for three pawns, so grabbing the clean pawn is better.

Black's queen on a2 is completely undefended, and Rxa2 simply takes it; I calculated the only follow-up, 13...Bxd2+ 14.Kxd2, which nets me queen plus bishop (12) for my queen (9), leaving me a bishop ahead with Nc3 and Bd4 still strong. Nxa2 reaches the same material but strands the knight on the rim, so the rook capture is better.

I'm down a queen for a pawn after the unfortunate Qxa2 adventure, so my only hope is to coordinate my pieces quickly, keep the bishop pair, and avoid further material loss. Nxe5 just drops a knight to Bxe5/fxe5, and Bc5 invites a trade that helps the queen side, so I'll castle to safety and connect my rooks while keeping d5 solidly defended by e6.

I'm already a queen for a pawn ahead, so I checked for Black checks (none available) and then counted the a7 capture: 14.Bxa7 Rxa7 15.Rxa7 nets rook for bishop, whereas the immediate 14.Rxa7?? Rxa7 would just lose a rook. Black's best is 14...Bc5 15.Bxc5 Nxc5, after which I've pocketed the a-pawn and kept my overwhelming material edge with everything defended.

I'm down a queen for a pawn, so I need practical chances: 14...b6 shuts the a7-g1 diagonal and, with my knight on d7 covering b8, the bishop on a7 has no escape square at all. If White doesn't rush to defend it with Nb5, I can add a second attacker with Nb8-c6 and win the bishop back; against 15.Qa5 I can hold b6 with Bc5.

The Bb4 is only kept out of d2 by my knight on c3, so any knight move (e.g. Nxd5) runs into ...Bxd2+ trading bishop for queen — I avoid that entirely. My a7-bishop is attacked by Ra8 and has no safe retreat (Bb8 Rxb8, Bxb6 Nxb6), so instead of losing time I develop with 15.Bb5: it prepares castling, is untouchable (no ...a6), and after ...Rxa7 Rxa7 my rook and bishop both hit the Nd7 which only Bc8 defends.

I'm down a queen for two pawns, so I need maximum practical counterplay: the key features are that White's Ba7 is trapped (only b8, where Ra8 takes it) and that Nc3 is effectively pinned, since any knight move allows Bxd2+ winning the queen for a bishop. Nc5 keeps that pin, activates the knight toward e4/b3, and prepares ...Ba6 so that Bxa6 Rxa6 (or any bishop retreat) leaves a7 falling to my doubled attackers.

I'm a full queen up, so the priority is safety and not dropping material: 16.Bxb6 fails to ...Rxa2 (my rook on a2 is undefended), and Ra3/Ra4/Ra5/Ra6 all drop the rook to Bxa3, Nxa4, bxa5 or Nxa6/Bxa6. Castling tucks the king away from any Nd3+/Ne4 tricks, activates the h-rook, and next move I can play Ra1 so that Bxb6 (hitting the c5 knight) works with a safe recapture on the a-file.

I'm down a queen, so I need to create threats: Ne4 hits both the c3 knight and the undefended queen on d2, and the natural 17.Nxe4 fails to 17...Bxd2 since the c3 square opens for my bishop, winning the queen back. Otherwise White must move the queen and I can take on c3, and if bxc3 then Bxc3 picks up a pawn.

My queen on d2 is attacked twice (Ne4 and Bb4) and undefended, and 17.Nxe4 loses to 17...Bxd2, so I must move the queen while keeping Nc3 protected. Qd3 is a square no black piece attacks, it defends c3 (and c3 again after bxc3, so ...Nxc3 bxc3 Bxc3 Qxc3 just wins a piece), and it also pressures the Ne4 while I stay up a queen for a rook.

I'm a queen down, so I must avoid further losses and keep my pieces active: every other knight move drops material (Nd6/Nf6 to exd6/exf6, Ng5 to fxg5, Nd2/Nf2/Ng3 are simply taken), while Nc5 is attacked by nothing (Ba7's diagonal is blocked by my b6 pawn) and hits the queen with tempo. It also keeps White's Ba7 entombed — it can only go to b8 — so Ra2 stays tied to its defence, which is why I avoid trading my good bishop with Bc5+.

My queen on d3 is attacked by the Nc5 and the c2 pawn is not a real defender (Nxd3 cxd3 wins Q for N), so I must move it; I checked Qxd5 and Nxd5 and both lose the queen to ...exd5/...Nxd3, so instead I centralize with Qd4, which is attacked by nothing (Bb4's diagonal misses d4, and ...Nb3 just loses a knight to cxb3) while hitting the loose Bb4 and the Nc5.

My bishop on b4 is attacked by the queen and undefended, while the knight on c5 is safely covered by the b6 pawn. Retreats like Ba3 or Ba5 lose material to Rxa2-file tricks (Rxa3, or Qxc5 bxc5 then Rxa5), and Ne4 drops the bishop after Nxe4 dxe4 Qxb4, so I'll trade bishop for knight to damage White's queenside pawns and keep pressure on the loose a7 bishop.

Qxc5 and Qxd5 both lose material because b6 and e6 pawns recapture, and Bxb6 drops my queen to Bxd4+, so I simply recapture on c3 with the pawn. bxc3 keeps my queen active on d4 (guarding c3), leaves my Ba7 defended by Ra2 against Rxa7, and keeps me a full queen for a knight ahead; Black's ...Na4 loses to Bxa4 and ...Nd3 to cxd3.

I'm down a queen for a pawn after my earlier ...Qxa2 blunder, so I need to stop the bleeding: White's immediate threat is Bxb6, picking up the pawn and hitting my knight a second time. Rb8 defends b6 (Bxb6 Rxb6 would lose the bishop), keeps my knight solidly supported on c5, and simultaneously entombs the bishop on a7, which now has no squares at all (b8 occupied, b6 covered).

The a7 bishop is deep in Black's camp and b8 is a loose rook — Rf8 can't recapture because its own bishop blocks c8, and no pawn or piece covers b8, so Bxb8 simply wins a whole rook. I checked Black's counters: there are no checks, and Nd3/Nb3 just drop the knight to cxd3/cxb3 while Nd7 hitting my bishop is met by Ba7 with Nxe5 losing to fxe5.

My knight on c5 is hanging to Qxd4-c5, so it must move, and Nd7 is the best square: it's defended by my bishop on c8 and it attacks the undefended bishop on b8 as well as the e5 pawn. If White plays Bxd7 Bxd7 I at least trade a pair of pieces and relieve some pressure.

My b8 bishop is attacked by Nd7, so I must address it; Qxd5 and Qxb6 both fail (exd5 wins my queen, Nxb8 wins the bishop), so instead of just trading with Bxd7 I retreat to c7, a square no black piece (pawn, rook, bishop or knight) touches, which keeps both bishops and piles a second attacker on the undefended b6 pawn that Black cannot cover (Rb8 is blocked by his own Bc8).

My knight on d7 is my only loose piece and every knight move loses it (exf6, Bxb8, Qxc5, fxe5), so I must add a defender instead. Rd8 backs up the knight, keeps b6 covered by the knight, and after Bxd7 Rxd7 my rook hits the c7 bishop, regaining some activity.

My bishop on c7 already attacks the rook on d8, and I verified d8 is guarded by nothing — the king is on g8, the Bc8 doesn't cover d8 and the Nd7 can't defend it either, so Bxd8 simply wins a whole rook with no recapture. I rejected Qxd5 because the e6 pawn recaptures and drops my queen, and Bxd7 only trades pieces instead of grabbing the free rook.

My bishop on c8 is the only defender of the knight on d7, so Ba6 or Bb7 just drops the knight to Bxd7, and Nxe5 loses a piece to Qxe5 or fxe5. Nf6 moves the knight to safety, offers a trade of White's extra bishop, and frees my c8 bishop for the next move.

Qxd5 is a trap since the e6 pawn recaptures, so I checked defenders first; instead Bxf6 removes Black's only active piece and simplifies while I'm up a queen and two rooks for a knight, and gxf6 exf6 shatters the black king's cover for a quick finish.

I'm down massive material and White's bishop on f6 is the key attacker against my king, so I need to eliminate it rather than allow Bxg7 with my position collapsing. Capturing with gxf6 removes one bishop and keeps my king covered for the moment, even though White remains winning after exf6.

I'm up a queen, two rooks and a bishop for a bishop, so my only job is to avoid a tactic: Qxd5 loses the queen to exd5, so I rejected it per my rule about counting every capturer of the destination square. Qxb6 wins a clean pawn, keeps my b5 bishop defended by the queen, and Black has no checks or captures at all in reply.

I'm down a huge amount of material, so I must avoid losing more: Bd7 drops the bishop to Qb8+, Bb7 is taken at once by the queen, and Ba6 falls to Rxa6 since a6 is undefended. Kg7 keeps my bishop guarded by the king, takes the back rank away from Qb8+, and keeps my pawn chain intact.

Qxe6 looks tempting but the c8 bishop guards e6 (via d7), so that would just trade my queen for a pawn — rule 2 forbids it. Instead Qc7 attacks the undefended bishop on c8 and the f7 pawn along the seventh rank, and every bishop retreat (Bd7, Bb7, Ba6) is met by Bxd7 or Qxb7/Bxa6, so I simply win the last black piece with no checks or captures available to Black.

My bishop on c8 is attacked by the queen and has no safe square (Bb7 Qxb7, Bd7 Bxd7, Ba6 Bxa6), so it's lost whatever I do in this already hopeless material situation. I'll play Ba6 so that at least White's strong light-squared bishop gets drawn away to the edge on a6 when it captures, giving my king a bit more breathing room.

Black's bishop on a6 is completely undefended and my bishop on b5 attacks it, so Bxa6 wins a whole piece for free, leaving Black with only pawns against my queen, two rooks and bishop. I checked that Black has no checks or captures at all in reply, and taking with the bishop (rather than Rxa6) keeps both rooks for a quick finish.

I'm down a queen's worth of material with only king and pawns left, so my priority is king safety and avoiding immediate tactics. Captures like fxe5 only open the f-file for White's rook against my f7 pawn, so I tuck the king to g8 where it defends f7 and stays off the dark-square diagonals and the g-file.

I almost played Qxf7+, but f7 is defended by nothing of mine and Black's king simply takes — exactly the "don't land on a square the enemy king attacks" mistake. Instead 27.Qd8+ forces 27...Kg7 (h8 and f8 are covered, f7 is blocked), and then 28.Qxf6+ is safe because my e5 pawn guards f6, after which Rf3-g3 and Qg7 mates.
I'm in check from the queen on d8 and Kg7 is the only legal move, so there's nothing to calculate — forced.

I'm up a queen, two rooks and a bishop against bare pawns, so I just need the fastest forced mate; Qxf6+ is safe because my e5 pawn guards f6, and the king must go to g8 (g7-escapes h6/h8 are covered by the queen). Then Ra8 is mate since g7 is covered by the queen and h7 is blocked by Black's own pawn.

I must move the king out of check, and after Kg8 White gets a free tempo with Qxe6+ (hitting my king again and grabbing the e-pawn), whereas with Kf8 the king stays beside f7 and Qxe6 comes without check. Keeping the pawn defended and avoiding further checks is my best practical try in this lost position.

Black has only a bare king and pawns, so I just need a mating net: with my queen on f6 covering e7 and g7, a rook landing on the back rank is mate, so 29.Rb1 threatens 30.Rb8#. The king must step to e8 or g8 (any pawn move allows Rb8#), and after 29...Kg8 30.Rb8+ Kg7 31.Qxf7+ or 31.Rb7 the attack crashes through, with zero counterplay against my own king.

Every other move loses instantly to Rb8#, since my king on f8 (or g8) has no flight square — g7 and f8 are covered by the queen on f6 and h7/h6 don't help. Ke8 is the only move that avoids immediate mate, giving my king a path via d7 after Rb8+.

Black has only a bare king with pawns, so I look for forced mate: Bb5+ checks along b5-e8, and d7 is covered by the bishop while d8 and e7 are covered by Qf6, leaving only Kf8, after which Rb8 is mate (g7 and e7 are guarded by the queen, f7 is Black's own pawn). The bishop on b5 is untouchable and no pawn can block, so this forces mate in two.
Only one legal move is available — the bishop check on b5 forces my king back to f8, as Kd7 and Ke7 would be illegal or covered.

Ra8 delivers check along the empty eighth rank, and the king's only flights e7 and g7 are both covered by my queen on f6 while f7 is blocked by Black's own pawn — nothing can capture or interpose on a8.

new_lessons: [middlegame] Before any quiet or developing move, list every enemy check; if a check wins a loose piece (Qa5+/Qh4+ hitting a stray knight or bishop), choose another move. Example: 11.Bc4?? Qh4+ 12.Bf2 Qxc4: f3 plus uncastled king made the e1-h4 check decisive, 55%→8%

[middlegame] Count all attackers and defenders of the target square and play the whole recapture chain to its end; move only if the final material count favours you. Example: ...Qc3 "forked" rooks but bxc3 won the queen; 26.Ne5 Rxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 gave two knights for a rook

[middlegame] Every move, name your undefended pieces and the entry squares (c2, d3, g4, your 6th/7th rank) an enemy piece can reach; guard the loosest first. Example: Loose bishop plus loose pawn gave Black free tempi ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5; the rook then invaded d6-c6

[opening] When a developed piece is attacked, prefer a pawn block that also defends your centre over retreating the piece to its starting square. Example: 8...Qa5+ : 9.Nc3 undeveloped the knight; 9.c3 held d4 and kept the pawn mass, 57%→53%

[middlegame] When a bishop pins your knight against king or loose rook, kick the pinner with a3/h3 (or Bd2) rather than passively defending with the queen. Example: 12.Qd2 let ...Nc5-e4 pile on; 12.a3 questioned Bb4 at once, 59%→54%

[middlegame] When your queen is attacked by an enemy piece you can capture, calculate the capture first; losing queen for the attacking pieces is fine when it nets material. Example: 17.Qd3 shuffled; 17.Nxe4 Bxd2 was better since I was already a queen for a rook up

[middlegame] Keep a knight or bishop on an advanced central square only if a pawn can support it; retreat before enemy pawns take away every square. Example: Unsupported Ne4 had no safe retreat after e5/d6; Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns

[middlegame] Never push pawns in front of your castled king while an enemy bishop or queen eyes those squares; meet a wing storm with a central break instead. Example: 17.g3 invited fxg3 and Bxh3; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[opening] Delay the central break (d5/e5) until your minor pieces are out and your king is castled; opened lines favour the better developed side. Example: 8...d5 exd5 with Nb8 and king home left a backward e5 pawn and open e-file, 48%→42%

[opening] When two pieces can recapture, use the minor piece; recapturing with the queen onto a square the enemy queen eyes hands over a free trade and a tempo. Example: 10...Qxd5? 11.Qxd5 Bxd5 reached the same structure a tempo down with queens gone, 45%→38%

[opening] Before starting an exchange sequence on an open file, recount the defenders of your central pawns after every single trade, not just the first. Example: 8.a4 axb5 axb5 Rxa8 removed e4's guard and lost the pawn to ...Nxe4

[endgame] Never put a piece on a square the enemy king attacks unless you guard it; check Kx-captures and stalemate before every move, even in won positions. Example: 66...Qc3+? Kxc3 drew a won queen endgame; earlier 58...Rd4 allowed 60.Kxd4

[endgame] When material ahead, accept every equal trade and simplify; rook plus pawns beats bishop plus pawns, and only bare rook versus bishop is drawn. Example: Refusing 31.Rd5 trade "to keep the exchange" dropped winning chances 94%→61%

[endgame] With extra material, first cut off the enemy king and seize the seventh rank; advance a pawn only when king or rook escorts it. Example: 59...b5 pushed an unescorted pawn instead of Rd5; loose pawns let the king counterattack

[endgame] Keep extra pawns connected and mutually defended, and before grabbing material check your king stays inside the square of every enemy passer. Example: 29...dxc4 scattered a6/c4/c6; 44...Kxh4 won a rook but f4-f5-f6 plus the h-pawn made two queens
